summary: For ages 6-7, this topic develops the full mathematical modelling cycle: represent a money or measurement word problem with a number sentence, bar model, or diagram, AND complete the 'return trip' by interpreting the numerical answer back in context with its unit ('5p change', '15 cm long') and checking whether it is reasonable. The defining new demand is that a bare number is not an answer; the remedy to 'suspension of sense-making' is to reason about the situation before computing and always interpret and sense-check the result afterwards.
misconceptions: Stops at a bare number without interpreting it in context or attaching a unit
Grabs the numbers and applies the operation a keyword suggests, without modelling the situation
Doesn't sense-check — accepts an answer that can't be true in the situation (change larger than the money paid)
Reports the wrong quantity (gives the total when the question asks for what's left)

activities.title: Model a shop story, then make the return trip
steps: Read a shop story, e.g. 'Sam has 20p in his purse and buys a sticker costing 15p. How much change does he get?'
Build a bar model of the situation: 20 as the whole, split into a 15 part and a mystery (change) part; or write a matching number sentence.
Work out the missing part to land on 5.
Complete a mandatory 'what does your 5 mean?' step: attach the unit and quantity, finishing the sentence '5p change'.
Pass a reasonableness check before the answer is accepted: decide whether a candidate answer could possibly be true in the story (e.g. flag that change greater than the amount paid is impossible).
activities.insight: A calculation is not finished when the number appears; it is finished when the number is read back into the story and checked for whether it could possibly be true. You cannot end up with MORE money after spending some.

activities.title: Argue with the shopkeeper: catch the impossible change
steps: Talk with a shopkeeper character (role-played by a partner, teacher, or on-screen character) who offers a plausible-sounding but impossible answer: 'You gave me 20p for a 15p sticker, so your change is 35p, right?'
Decide out loud whether 35p can be right, and explain why change cannot be larger than the money paid.
State the correct change in context ('5p change') and justify it.
Respond to a follow-up: 'If the sticker cost 25p, could Sam buy it with his 20p? How do you know?'
activities.insight: Defending why an answer does or does not make sense out loud strengthens the reasonableness habit; a contrasting impossible answer provokes the check that compute-and-stop skips.

activities.title: Bar models for part-whole and comparison problems
steps: Draw a part-whole bar model for a word problem, labelling which part is the known quantity, which is the whole, and which is the unknown.
Use a comparison bar model to show two quantities side by side for a comparison problem (e.g. one ribbon longer than another).
Use a number line to represent money or measurement jumps when that fits the story better.
Attach units to each quantity on the model and to the final answer.
activities.insight: Bar models expose the structure of a situation — including part-whole and comparison relationships — so the child models the relationships rather than grabbing numbers and applying a keyword operation.

checkQuestion: Sam has 20p. He buys a sticker that costs 15p. A friend worked it out and said the answer is 35. Does 35 make sense as Sam's change? Talk me through it — what should the answer be, and what does that number mean for Sam?
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child rejecting 35 as impossible (you can't have more money after spending), finding 5, and interpreting it as '5p change', not a bare number.
